To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the localization of a target in darkness is determined by a combination of the position of each eye in the orbit (the position of each eye is measured by the proprioceptors in each orbit, and the information is transmitted to the brain by the oculomotor nerves), and the relative position of the two eyes (the relative position of the eyes is measured by the muscles that move the eyes and the information is conveyed to the brain by efferent signals).

the direction in which a visual target seems to be is determined by the direction in which the eye is actually pointing, and that the direction of the target is not judged relative to the direction of the eye, but rather to the direction in which it is intended to move.

the direction of a visual target seen by an unaided eye is determined by a combination of afferent and proprioceptor input, and the direction of a single target is determined by the position of both eyes in the orbits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of proprioception in the localization of a visual target in space by an eye that moves.
the question whether visual localization of targets is based on the coding of the eye's position in the orbit or on the coding of its movement.
the role of eye muscle proprioceptors in visual localization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the localization of a single target in darkness depends upon the proprioceptive input of both orbits and that the proprioceptive input is not only from the eye that sees the target.
the mechanism of visual localization of a single stationary point target in the dark is a function of afferent and different signals from all the active muscles.
the localization of a visual target depends on the position of the eyes in the orbit, and on the direction of gaze.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the visual localization mechanism in man is based on afferent signals from both the ipsilateral and the contralateral orbits and that the efferent signals of all the muscles involved in ocular movements play a role in the localization process.
the visual direction judgement mechanism is based on the combined input from afferent and motor efferent information from all muscles involved in the eye movements.
the direction of a visual target is determined from the combined information from the eye and the extraocular muscles, and not from the position of the eyes in the orbit.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain uses the proprioception of the muscles to localize targets in darkness.

proprioception of eye position is a critical component in the process of determining target location in space, and that this is not a function of the visual system alone, but is a function of the whole motor system.
the brain uses the proprioceptive information from all the muscles of the eye to localize the target.
